definition: In statistics, ordinal regression, also called ordinal classification, is a type of regression analysis used for predicting an ordinal variable, i.e.
details: a variable whose value exists on an arbitrary scale where only the relative ordering between different values is significant. It can be considered an intermediate problem between regression and classification. Examples of ordinal regression are ordered logit and ordered probit. Ordinal regression turns up often in the social sciences, for example in the modeling of human levels of preference (on a scale from, say, 1–5 for "very poor" through "excellent"), as well as in information retrieval. In machine learning, ordinal regression may also be called ranking learning.

explainer.lead: Ordinal regression, also called ordinal classification, predicts a variable whose values have a meaningful order but arbitrary spacing. It matters because it sits between regression and classification and appears often where human judgments are graded.

tiers.eli5: It is for answers that come in a ranked order, like a rating from very poor to excellent, where the steps between labels are not fixed amounts.
tiers.practitioner: It is used in the social sciences to model human levels of preference, such as a 1–5 scale, and in information retrieval. Ordered logit and ordered probit are examples; a pitfall is treating the scale as if the distances between values were meaningful.
tiers.paperLevel: A type of regression analysis for predicting an ordinal variable, one whose value lies on an arbitrary scale where only relative ordering is significant; examples are ordered logit and ordered probit.

explainer.example: Survey respondents rate a product from 1 (very poor) to 5 (excellent), and an ordered logit model predicts which rating level a respondent falls into.
